introduction: After Cyrus’s death, negotiations promise a way out. Clearchus trusts Tissaphernes’ invitation despite objections in the Greek camp. The meeting ends with the generals captured and captains outside killed. Their capture and their later deaths are separate events.

Source: Xenophon, Anabasis 2.5.25–35; 2.6 for the generals’ later fates. This is a controlled Attic Greek course adaptation, not a verbatim ancient extract. Sequence, persons, and historical outcomes follow the sources; sentence wording, compact transitions, and quoted speech are course compositions. Historical speakers are not being quoted verbatim.

Aorist narrative is now a target. Blue glosses identify lexical irregularities and forms beyond this lesson: imperfects, passive or athematic aorists, perfect participles, and unfamiliar infinitives remain supported exposure rather than assessed production. Comparison passages from Memorabilia belong to a separate work and setting.

reading.translation:
After Cyrus’s death, the Greeks entered negotiations with Tissaphernes. Clearchus spoke about the route and trust. Tissaphernes invited the generals.

Some of the soldiers saw the danger. They said to Clearchus: “All the leaders must not go together.” Clearchus, however, trusted Tissaphernes.

Five generals and twenty captains came to the doors. The generals entered, while the captains remained outside. Socrates the Achaean went with the generals; this man is not the Athenian philosopher.

The captains remained at the doors. The enemies seized the generals and killed the captains. Xenophon speaks elsewhere about the generals’ later deaths.

The soldiers in camp saw the horsemen. They did not learn what had happened immediately. Nicarchus came to them wounded and told the news.

On hearing the news, the Greeks ran to their arms. The generals are no longer in camp, but the soldiers still have weapons. They must take new counsel.

wordStudy.label: Word Study — Trust and the language of command

blocks.title: Trust and the language of command
body: πίστις names trust; πιστεύω names the action of trusting, commonly with a dative person. In τῷ Τισσαφέρνει ἐπίστευσεν the dative tells us whom Clearchus trusted. The word’s meaning does not prove that the trust was justified.

στρατηγός and λοχαγός name distinct offices: general and company captain. Tracking these nouns preserves the different immediate fates at the meeting. A στρατηγός is not simply a synonym for every military leader.
σῆμα is a signal; ἀγγελία is a report. A signal can coordinate action while a report informs the distant camp. εἶδον and εἶπον connect seeing and telling to different dictionary verbs, ὁράω and λέγω.

grammar.intro: Use the story to identify who acts and how the action is presented. The following 4 sections teach each assigned topic separately, with forms, worked examples, checks, and practice.
objectives: εἶπον and εἶδον: unrelated stems: explain the pattern and interpret its worked examples.
Second-aorist commands and accent exceptions: explain the pattern and interpret its worked examples.
Syllabic and temporal augment: explain the pattern and interpret its worked examples.
Indicative, participle, and imperative: explain the pattern and interpret its worked examples.

sections.title: 1. εἶπον and εἶδον: unrelated stems
body: A dictionary verb can supply a quite different aorist stem. λέγω, “I say,” has the common aorist εἶπον, “I said”; ὁράω, “I see,” has εἶδον, “I saw.” These are thematic second aorists because of their formation and endings, despite the surprising stems.

Keep the assigned principal parts together: λέγω–ἐρῶ–εἶπον and ὁράω–ὄψομαι–εἶδον. Present and future forms cannot be used as instructions for inventing the aorist. Learn both recognition and the return from a reading form to its dictionary entry.

εἶπον and εἶδον each can be first singular or third plural. εἶπεν and εἶδεν are third singular; εἴπομεν and εἴδομεν are first plural. The alternative aorist εἶπα occurs in Greek but is not the production pattern assigned here.

examples.greek: οἱ στρατιῶται τὸν κίνδυνον εἶδον καὶ εἶπον.
examples.english: The soldiers saw the danger and spoke.

checks.prompt: What dictionary verb lies behind εἶπον?
checks.answer: λέγω. The principal parts connect λέγω and εἶπον.

checks.prompt: What dictionary verb lies behind εἶδον?
checks.answer: ὁράω. The principal parts connect ὁράω and εἶδον.

sections.title: 2. Second-aorist commands and accent exceptions
body: Aorist commands present the requested action as a whole. Many active second singular forms are recessive, as φύγε, “flee,” from φεύγω. Commands lack the indicative augment: contrast indicative ἔφυγε with imperative φύγε.

Five familiar simple active second-aorist imperatives have exceptional final accent: εἰπέ, ἐλθέ, εὑρέ, ἰδέ, λαβέ. Standard Attic simple λαβέ belongs among these exceptions; use this accented form for the assigned singular command. The contrast is φύγε, whose accent is recessive.

The corresponding plurals are εἴπετε, ἔλθετε, εὕρετε, ἴδετε, λάβετε; the singular exception does not carry over to the plural. Before another word, final acute normally becomes grave: εἰπέ → εἰπὲ τὴν ἀλήθειαν. Compound imperatives generally revert to recessive accent, as ἄπελθε; full compound augment is next lesson’s later topic.
The commands in the table are supplementary course examples. They are not quotations attributed to Clearchus or Nicarchus.

examples.greek: εἰπὲ τὴν ἀλήθειαν· ἴδετε τοὺς ἱππέας.
examples.english: Tell the truth; look at the horsemen.

checks.prompt: Which isolated command means “say!” to one person?
checks.answer: εἰπέ. εἰπέ is the exceptional oxytone singular imperative.

checks.prompt: Which isolated command means “see!” to one person?
checks.answer: ἰδέ. ἰδέ has exceptional final accent.

sections.title: 3. Syllabic and temporal augment
body: For many consonant-initial verbs, past indicative augment adds a syllable ἐ-: λαμβάνω → ἔλαβον, φεύγω → ἔφυγον. This syllabic augment is separate from changes in the aorist stem.

For vowel-initial verbs, temporal augment commonly lengthens the initial vowel: α and ε become η, ο becomes ω. Thus ἀκούω has ἤκουσα and ἐθέλω has ἠθέλησα. These first-aorist forms are supplied to illustrate augment, with their full formation postponed to Lesson 23.

Initial αι and οι commonly become ῃ and ῳ, while αυ commonly becomes ηυ; some verbs vary or have historically exceptional forms. Long vowels do not become “doubly long.” εἶδον is a learned irregular form, not evidence that every ε-initial verb becomes ει. Use a dictionary’s principal parts for exceptions.

examples.english: I heard the report; ἀ- has lengthened to ἠ-.

checks.prompt: What kind of augment occurs in ἔφυγον?
checks.answer: syllabic. ἐ- adds a syllable before the consonant.
temporal. The initial α of ἀκούω lengthens to η.

sections.title: 4. Indicative, participle, and imperative
body: Augment belongs to past indicatives in the system taught here. Compare εἶδον, “I saw / they saw,” with ἰδών, “having seen,” and ἰδέ, “see!” Their different forms guide you to different functions.

Participles agree like adjectives: ἰδών, ἰδοῦσα, ἰδόν. Imperatives address the hearer. Infinitives such as ἰδεῖν and εἰπεῖν name the action without a personal ending. None of these nonindicative forms receives the past indicative augment.

An unaugmented aorist is still an aorist stem. Removing augment changes neither its whole-action viewpoint nor automatically turns it into a present. In ἰδὼν τὸν κίνδυνον εἶπεν, the seeing is interpreted before the speaking by context.

examples.greek: ἰδὼν τὸν κίνδυνον ὁ στρατιώτης εἶπεν.
examples.english: Having seen the danger, the soldier spoke.

checks.prompt: Which form is an unaugmented participle?
checks.answer: ἰδών. ἰδών is a nominative masculine participle.

summary.title: Grammar Summary
items: εἶπον and εἶδον: unrelated stems: A dictionary verb can supply a quite different aorist stem. λέγω, “I say,” has the common aorist εἶπον, “I said”; ὁράω, “I see,” has εἶδον, “I saw.” These are thematic second aorists because of their formation and endings, despite the surprising stems.

Second-aorist commands and accent exceptions: Aorist commands present the requested action as a whole. Many active second singular forms are recessive, as φύγε, “flee,” from φεύγω. Commands lack the indicative augment: contrast indicative ἔφυγε with imperative φύγε.

Syllabic and temporal augment: For many consonant-initial verbs, past indicative augment adds a syllable ἐ-: λαμβάνω → ἔλαβον, φεύγω → ἔφυγον. This syllabic augment is separate from changes in the aorist stem.

Indicative, participle, and imperative: Augment belongs to past indicatives in the system taught here. Compare εἶδον, “I saw / they saw,” with ἰδών, “having seen,” and ἰδέ, “see!” Their different forms guide you to different functions.

sections.title: Oaths, negotiations, and risk
body: Anabasis presents the negotiations against a background of oaths and mutual suspicion. Clearchus treats the proposed meeting as a way to identify those spreading accusations. Trust in an agreement can have practical value, but the text also records soldiers who object.

Those objections concern concentrating the leaders in one place and trusting Tissaphernes. A leader’s confidence is therefore not the only voice available in the source. Ask what information and safeguards a decision needs, without claiming that the recorded objectors predicted every later event.

sections.title: Generals and captains are different offices
body: A στρατηγός is a general; a λοχαγός commands a company. At the meeting five generals enter while twenty captains wait outside. The simultaneous attack gives the two groups different immediate fates: seizure within, killing outside.

The capture removes important commanders but does not physically dissolve the Greek army. The camp still contains soldiers, arms, and surviving officers. Socrates the Achaean belongs to this military group; he must never be confused with the philosopher Socrates of Athens.

sections.title: Evidence and the order of events
body: From camp, the Greeks first see alarming movements without knowing their cause. Nicarchus’s arrival supplies a report. The reading suppresses graphic details of his injury while preserving his role as a wounded survivor and messenger.

Anabasis 2.6 discusses the captured generals’ later fates and character. That retrospective chapter must not be collapsed into an execution at the meeting’s doors. An accurate account can be compact while retaining the distinction between capture, immediate killings, and later death.

questions.prompt: Why record the objections?
questions.answer: they show dissent within the army. The source preserves more than Clearchus’s confidence.

questions.prompt: What does λοχαγός mean here?
questions.answer: company captain. A captain differs from a general.

questions.prompt: Which distinction protects the chronology?
questions.answer: capture now versus later fates. The later retrospective chapter is a separate stage.

questions.prompt: What remains after the betrayal?
questions.answer: soldiers, arms, and surviving officers. The army must reorganize; it has not dissolved.

questions.prompt: What changes the camp’s information?
questions.answer: a survivor’s report. Nicarchus reports what the watching soldiers did not know.

questions.prompt: What should trust be evaluated alongside?
questions.answer: information and safeguards. The culture page connects trust with responsible judgment.
